#5439. Microsoft jabs at OpenAI and Anthropic, touting cheaper, customizable AI models of its own

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 11:57 amNovember 17, 2026 at 12:33 pm

Microsoft is a partner and investor in both OpenAI and Anthropic, and it sells their AI models to its own customers. But another role was on full display during the company’s Ignite keynote Tuesday: competitor.

“Simply stated, anything you can do in Claude or ChatGPT, you can do better with Copilot and for less,” said Judson Althoff, CEO of Microsoft’s commercial business, during the opening keynote at the company’s annual conference for IT professionals and business customers in San Francisco.

Jacob Andreou, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, went further. “We’ve all seen Anthropic and OpenAI embrace documents, slides, and spreadsheets, but their simplified viewers and editors force compromise on power and collaboration,” he said.

The full versions of Word, Excel and PowerPoint inside Copilot are included in the subscription. “That means that Copilot is the only way to draft a PowerPoint presentation without spinning a meter,” Andreou said.

Microsoft’s cost comparison: Andreou backed up the pitch with a chart of estimated monthly costs per business user, including subscription and usage fees. It put Copilot at $30 for an “everyday” AI user, compared with $81 for ChatGPT and $205 for Claude.

For “advanced” users of each company’s agent tools, it showed $96 for Copilot, $149 for ChatGPT and $299 for Claude. Most of the Claude figure is estimated usage charges on top of Anthropic’s $20 enterprise seat.

The numbers come from research Microsoft commissioned and paid for from GigaOm, based on testing Microsoft ran in October on modeled workloads. They reflect enterprise pricing, which adds usage charges to a per-seat fee, not the flat monthly subscriptions that individuals pay for ChatGPT and Claude.

Partners and rivals: The pitch comes as Anthropic expands into Microsoft’s core business. Last week it introduced new Claude-based tools for spreadsheets and whiteboards that compete more directly with Office. The company is expected to make its IPO this week, putting new scrutiny on its financials and long-term growth prospects.

The companies’ products are also intertwined. Anthropic’s Claude for Microsoft 365, for example, lets people use Claude inside Office apps for tasks such as sorting email and creating slide decks.

The product has less than a tenth as many weekly users as the paid version of Copilot in Office, The Information reported Monday, citing internal Microsoft data. Andreou is one of the executives who see that as a sign Microsoft can keep customers from switching, the report said.

New MAI models: Microsoft AI also released a new batch of its own MAI models, built to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic for a fraction of the price. It’s a notable stance, given that Microsoft still sells their models, too. On the same stage, CEO Satya Nadella announced that OpenAI’s GPT-6.2, released Tuesday morning, is now available in Microsoft Foundry.

The lineup includes MAI Code 2, available in GitHub Copilot starting Tuesday. Microsoft says it delivers 96% of the coding performance of Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the price, on benchmarks Microsoft chose.

Microsoft also introduced MAI Cyber 2 Flash, a security model it says matches OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra on one benchmark at less than 2% of the cost per task. Other new models cover image editing, live speech and transcription.

The other new business: MAI Licensed Weights. Companies can take a Microsoft AI model, customize it with their own data and run it in their own Azure environment, with help from Microsoft’s Frontier Company consulting arm. AT&T used an earlier version of the program, Custom Models, to build a MAI model for 5G network analytics.

It’s the latest step in Microsoft’s push for what Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has called “long term self-sufficiency,” which started with seven homegrown models at Build in June.

Keeping costs in check: The cost theme ran through the keynote. In a demo, Althoff showed Copilot building a keynote outline, a slide deck and a customer tracker for a retail conference, plus an agent he named Amelia to keep the work going.

The cost of his two-hour Sunday session: about 10,000 credits, or roughly $100. Althoff presented that as a bargain compared with the staff time it would have taken: “my team hits the ground running for NRF without me bothering them,” he said.

Microsoft is also selling tools to keep that bill in check. A new Agent 365 Business Analytics feature shows business leaders what’s driving their AI spending and what they’re getting for it, and a companion Cost Management tool lets IT set spending policies and get alerts. Microsoft cited a McKinsey survey in which 93% of respondents reported exceeding their AI budgets.

In another notable announcement, Microsoft and Salesforce unveiled “Copilotforce,” bringing Salesforce customer data and actions into Copilot, Teams and Fabric. The Copilot plugin is available in preview.

Earlier, Nadella opened the keynote by addressing last week’s global Outlook outage.

MediaTek powers more than two billion devices every year, from the most advanced AI infrastructure on the planet to the everyday devices that make life smarter, faster, and more connected. For everyone. MediaTek silicon is the common thread running through all of it. Yeah, MediaTek does that.

#5438. Seattle startup Aarden raises $8M to help landowners navigate the AI and energy building boom

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 1:36 pmNovember 20, 2026 at 5:15 pm

Seattle startup Aarden AI on Tuesday announced $8 million in new funding to grow its team and accelerate its work helping landowners evaluate potential uses for their properties and navigate deals with developers building data centers, clean energy projects, housing and other projects.

Founded last year, the company says its clients collectively own or manage approximately 14 million acres worldwide — nearly the land area of West Virginia. Aarden’s team said it has evaluated more than $500 million worth of land deals.

“But land markets remain opaque and manual with far too much friction. Finding the right site, and building trust with the right partners quickly, is more important than ever for our economy and our environment,” founder and CEO Danan Margason said in a statement.

The company combines data on hundreds of land attributes with historical market data and proprietary models to assess development suitability, valuation trends, ownership and community sentiment. Its tools and services also help developers identify sites and connect with landowners.

Aarden generates revenue through subscriptions to its technology, which includes AI-native data, models and investment tools, and through fees for services tied to specific deals or analyses.

The new funding brings Aarden’s total investments to $12 million. Overture Ventures led the round, with participation from Madrona and Propeller Ventures. The startup previously raised $4 million in a round led by Planeteer in June 2025. The company has 13 employees and plans to nearly double in size over the next 12 months.

Margason said he launched the business on the premise that while there have long been tools to support developers, landowners have been largely on their own to evaluate and optimize deals so they’re not taken advantage of or end up partnering with untrustworthy organizations.

One customer, timberland investment manager Resource Management Service, uses Aarden to evaluate whether tracts are best suited for continued timber production, conservation, solar development or other uses.

“Diligence that used to take months now produces investment-grade answers we can act on, and that is shaping how we manage value across our portfolio,” said Alex Hinson, president and CEO of Resource Management Service.

Other companies offering property research and analysis tools include Acres, which provides land data, valuations and due diligence tools, and Land id, which offers property insights and mapping tools.

Ben Eidelson, a partner at Stepchange Ventures, which participated in the startup’s first funding round, said the company is already having an impact.

“We now have the capability to make smarter decisions about land, optimizing for the outcomes that matter from conservation to the local economy,” Eidelson said on LinkedIn.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5437. CFTC Makes Historic Move With Blockchain Derivatives Approval

The U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened historic doors for blockchain technology adoption in traditional financial markets as it approves exchange and clearinghouse applications for blockchain-based derivatives market infrastructure.

On Nov. 16, CFTC Chairman Michael Selig announced that the commission had given the green light to exchange (designated contract market or DCM) and clearinghouse (derivatives clearing organization or DCO) applications for a company using blockchain technology for the execution and settlement of derivatives contracts.

As per the official statement, Selig considers this a major step forward for U.S. financial markets. He said that blockchain-based market infrastructure is compatible with current U.S. financial regulations.

"This approval makes clear that there is a regulatory path for companies that want to innovate and use blockchain technology to modernize how derivatives are traded and settled,"  he elaborated.

Selig pointed out that the U.S. derivatives markets have seen a number of technological advancements, from physical trading floors to electronic trading platforms.

Now, with blockchain technology, he believes there is an opportunity to further modernize financial market infrastructure without losing regulatory oversight and investor protections.

Notably, there is no technical architecture requirement imposed on derivatives exchanges and clearinghouses under the CFTC's current regulatory framework.

Therefore, firms that leverage blockchain-based networks can apply for regulatory approval under the same set of rules and regulations that apply to traditional financial market participants.

However, Selig also clarified that blockchain adoption is not a license to escape regulatory oversight.

Companies will still need to comply with rules covering anti-money laundering (AML), client protections, market monitoring, risk mitigation and other measures designed to protect the integrity of financial markets.

Simply put, the CFTC is looking to bring blockchain technology into regulated derivatives market infrastructure while maintaining the same standards as traditional financial market participants.

For some time, the CFTC chairman has been pushing for a scenario where U.S. companies developing emerging financial technologies can operate in the country without having to look to international markets.

The latest developments further reinforce the message that the U.S. is open for business for companies building blockchain-based financial market infrastructure, according to Selig.

#5436. She was a go-to Manhattan babysitter as a teen. Now she’s running a $100 million-a-year AI startup whose clients include the billionaire Koch family

From a nationwide FAA ground stop to Microsoft and Chase outages that disrupted millions of customers, a string of recent technology failures has highlighted the need to modernize aging infrastructure while raising new fears about the risks of an increasingly AI-dependent world.

But for Jaclyn Rice Nelson, cofounder and CEO of Tribe AI, that tension is exactly why businesses should embrace the technology—not run from it.

“I don’t think that anxiety around AI is unwarranted. I think it’s very real,” Nelson told Fortune.

“[AI] is ours to shape,” Nelson said. “And the only way you can shape it is if you understand it, and the only way you understand it is if you use it—and use it a lot.”

Nelson, 41, has built her business around helping companies do just that. Founded in 2019, Tribe AI has grown to a $100 million annual run rate by helping organizations—from Fortune 500s like Hyatt and MetLife to multibillion-dollar private conglomerates like Koch Industries—put AI to work.

Tribe said on Nov. 18 that its annualized revenue had crossed $100 million, up 3.8 times from a year earlier, as more clients moved AI projects out of the pilot stage. “The hard part is getting AI into production inside a complex business,” Nelson said in the announcement.

Nelson’s instinct to build something of her own predates the AI boom by decades.

She grew up in New York City with a single mother raising two children. After transitioning from teaching to business, her mother managed to send both kids to private school in Manhattan—a sacrifice that left a lasting impression on Nelson.

“It was someone in my life who had done really hard things, who I had seen do hard things, and who also refused to let things slip for me,” Nelson said.

That set Nelson in motion to seek her own financial independence. As a teenager, she started babysitting and grew the side hustle into what she once described as a “babysitting empire.”

“I became this trusted, fairly scarce asset,” she said, adding that she became the go-to babysitter for entire New York apartment buildings, with parents competing to book her on Saturday nights.

But beyond the money, it also taught her an early lesson in business: “Be the trusted person, be dependable.”

After graduating in 2008 with a degree in political science from the University of Michigan, Nelson then took a more traditional route to financial independence: Wall Street. She spent two years as an analyst at Citigroup, before moving to Silicon Valley to work for Google—and brought the same work ethic that had served her in banking.

“I moved to a new city where I didn’t really know anyone,” she said. “And so I just worked banking hours at Google. I was always like the person still in the office, waving my hand to get the light sensors to go back on.”

Her work ethic, and willingness to take on responsibilities outside her core role, led her to make a career jump to Google’s growth equity fund, CapitalG (then known as Google Capital) in 2015 as its first business-focused employee among a team of dozens of engineers. Three years later, she left to pursue an opportunity of her own, cofounding Tribe AI in 2019.

Since 2019, the company has grown to roughly 250 employees, after its team grew fivefold this year, the company said—all while raising less than $10 million in venture funding and reaching profitability.

As Tribe continues to expand, Nelson said she’s looking for people who are deeply curious about AI, willing to take on difficult challenges, and humble enough to recognize how much they still have to learn.

“You have to be kind of humbled by how little you know every day and motivated by learning and getting better,” she said.

One of Tribe AI’s major customers is Koch Industries, one of the world’s largest privately held companies. The business conglomerate employs about 130,000 people and generates more than $125 billion in annual revenue.

“There’s a lot of businesses that run through the smartest guy in the room telling people what to do. We are the opposite of that,” Chase Koch, executive vice president of origination and partnerships at Koch and son of Charles, told Fortune.

Koch wanted to bring its decades-old management philosophy—centered on bottom-up principles developed by founder Charles Koch—into the AI era. Working with Tribe, the project went from an idea to a launched product in just five months. The result is an AI-powered coaching tool designed to help employees put the principles into practice. Employees can describe a challenge at work and receive personalized guidance on how to approach it.

Chase Koch said he tried the tool himself after his boss told him he was taking on too many responsibilities. Talking through the problem with the AI helped him develop a plan to prioritize his work, delegate more effectively, and focus on his strengths.

For Nelson, the project and its speed points to a bigger opportunity for AI: making personalized coaching and development more accessible, without losing sight of the people it’s meant to help.

“The goal of this is not just to scale AI, it’s to make people better, to help them lean in on the things that they are going to be the most uniquely suited to do,” Nelson said. “I believe AI is giving people these superpowers, and this is a good example of that.”

For young professionals facing the same shift, Koch and Nelson had similar but straightforward advice: Figure out what makes you uniquely valuable, then learn how to use AI to make the most of it.

“If you understand the technology and how it works, what are the places you can use that power and strength to then change the trajectory of how it is used and the impact that it has on people and workforces and society?” Nelson said.

Koch echoed an emphasis on individual strengths: “Understand what your comparative advantage is. What is your gift combined with what you’re really passionate about learning and what gets you excited and gets you out of bed in the morning?”

Preston Fore is a reporter on Fortune's Success team.

#5435. ‘Do not search Amazon’: Meta’s Muse now shops elsewhere by default

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 2:36 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:45 am

Two months after Amazon slammed the door on Muse, the AI agent has stopped knocking.

The shopping skill that guides Muse, Meta’s personal AI agent, now tells it to “leave out Amazon unless the user asks for it,” according to the instructions Muse provides when asked. The instructions include a template brief for Muse’s browser that says, “Do not search Amazon.”

The change was spotted last week by Juozas Kaziukenas, founder of the e-commerce research firm Marketplace Pulse, who asked Muse for the text of its shopping skill and compared it with the version from the day before. He posted the before-and-after on Friday. GeekWire asked Muse for its shopping skill and got the same language.

“Amazon blocked Muse, so now Muse blocked Amazon,” Kaziukenas wrote on X.

Muse is also told not to name Amazon as a site to search in that browser brief, “even as an example,” unless the user asked for Amazon. The skill steers the agent to Walmart and Target for general goods, Best Buy for electronics, and Home Depot or Lowe’s for home improvement.

For Muse users, not much changes in practice. Amazon began blocking Muse in September, less than two weeks after Meta launched the agent, showing anyone who tried to shop through it a message saying continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use. Kaziukenas said any Amazon search would fail anyway because of the block.

What’s new is that Meta appears to be going along with what Amazon asked for. When it began blocking Muse, Amazon said it had asked Meta to “remove Amazon from the experience.” Meta hadn’t said publicly how it would respond.

Meta didn’t respond to an inquiry about the change. An Amazon spokesperson said the company had nothing to share.

Amazon objected that Muse didn’t identify itself when it browsed the site and appeared to capture and store customer credentials. Meta has said Muse has no visibility into people’s passwords or payment methods. The standoff set off a broader debate over who owns the customer relationship when an AI agent does the buying.

Since then, both sides have kept moving. More than 10 million people in the U.S. and Canada signed up for Muse in its first six weeks, Forbes reported, and Walmart, Best Buy, Sephora and Wayfair are among the retailers working with Meta on it.

The business stakes are high for Amazon. It generated more than $68 billion in advertising revenue last year, including sponsored products that appear as people browse its pages — ads a shopper might never see if an outside agent does the searching. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said Muse will take a small cut of the transactions it handles.

Amazon has fought this battle before, suing Perplexity last November over the shopping agent in its Comet browser. It’s now pressing that case in part on the same Conditions of Use it cited in blocking Muse.

On Amazon’s earnings call last month, CEO Andy Jassy said outside shopping agents aren’t making a meaningful dent in Amazon’s advertising business. “Few customers are doing much shopping this way yet,” he said, adding that the experience still isn’t great or more convenient than going straight to a retailer.

Jassy said Amazon expects to work with “horizontal agents,” general-purpose assistants like Muse, but believes its own Alexa for Shopping will be the main agent people use to shop Amazon. Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping in May, combining its Rufus shopping chatbot with the Alexa+ assistant.

It has since started letting some customers text Alexa to shop, much as people do with Muse.

Malicious JavaScript code snippets were planted on the websites of 178 organizations.

The exploit originated inside Optimizely's Web Experimentation platform, a tool that many large companies use for A/B testing, which means showing users multiple versions of a page to determine which one is more effective.

Report URI estimates that on November 16 the code sat in 188 of the 1,611 Optimizely snippets it crawled, and the real number is most likely higher.

Among the websites that could become victims of the hack are some of the largest names in the world: Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Fox News, Salesforce, GitLab, IKEA, HSBC, Equifax, Air France-KLM, Ledger and Peacock. BleepingComputer confirms that the script loads on many of them.

Essentially, the script's goal was to swap a wallet address on the page for the attacker's one, capture card numbers, take screenshots of pages and more. It was a whole stack of tools used to steal personal data, wallets and other assets.

According to Report URI, the attacker's wallets received about $7,040 within the first nine hours. That is a drop in the ocean considering the names involved, though the losses from card skimming are unknown. A card skimmer was added later that day, and a hidden iframe tried to load an iOS exploit chain on older iPhones.

Optimizely confirmed that an unauthorized party had exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to certain customer projects. How the flaw worked is yet to be confirmed.

If successful, it could become one of the largest supply-chain attacks we have ever witnessed. Considering the attack came from a third party, we might see one of the largest service migrations in the world, as none of the third-party services and libraries can be trusted nowadays if used through an API.

Cryptocurrency services delegate certain tasks to third-party providers all the time, so witnessing a similar situation in our field is more than a possibility.

For product owners: stay cautious and rethink the use of services prone to exploits. For users: stay vigilant and try not to put all your eggs in one basket.

#5433. How to finance nature

From debt-for-nature swaps to wildlife bonds, new financial deals are bringing private investors into conservation

A version of this article originally appeared in Quartz’s members-only Weekend Brief newsletter. Quartz members get access to exclusive newsletters and more. Sign up here.

Most people don’t think of going to a climate summit to close a financial deal. But this year’s U.N. climate summit is shaping up differently.

A week before COP31 was due to open in Antalya, Turkey, Bank of America . It backs companies that protect ecosystems, from supply-chain tracking to DNA-based wildlife monitoring.

Join 500,000+ readers who start their day with Quartz.

More deals making time was set up for the summit. The COP organizers are putting on a Finance Day that will cover how to make nature projects something investors can actually buy and a Nordic development fund has planned a session where climate funds would pitch investors directly.

There are several financial instruments for financing nature. The oldest and best known is the debt-for-nature swap. A country with heavy debt gets some of it bought at a discount, then renegotiated on better terms in exchange for spending part of the savings on conservation. Bolivia struck the first in 1987, which was worth $650,000.

The deals have grown since. Ecuador’s 2023 swap for the Galapagos Islands bought roughly $1.6 billion of its bonds for $656 million and freed about $450 million for conservation. Many of the biggest swaps relied on a safeguard. Guarantees from the U.S. government promised to repay investors if political turmoil interrupted payments, which made the new debt safe enough to buy.

The market went quiet for a while, with only about $6 billion in swaps with private capital being done from 2021 to 2024. Renewed interest returned in February, when Britain’s biggest asset manager, Legal & General, committed up to $1 billion to anchor a new generation of deals.

Bonds are another route, and come in a variety of setups. The World Bank’s “rhino bond” was one. In 2022 it raised $150 million from investors who gave up their interest payments, about $9 million in all, so the money could go to protecting black rhinos in two South African parks. Investors were due their principal back in March 2027, plus a bonus of up to $13.8 million if the rhino population grew.

Others looked more like ordinary business. Funds like the one with King Charles III put money into companies and expected a commercial return. Payments for ecosystem services, usually run by governments, rewarded the conservation of a forest or wetland, and environmental credits, which works like carbon offsets, sold verified conservation as a tradable certificate.

It's still early to judge how well many of these instruments work. Some of the biggest deals are only a few years old, and their conservation commitments will take much longer to measure.

But there's pressure to scale them: the market is being built against an enormous funding gap. Private finance classified as nature-related has grown from $9.4 billion in 2020 to $102 billion in 2024, but even that jump left a vast amount of conservation unfunded, with BloombergNEF estimating the debt swap market could be as large as $1 trillion.

The deals themselves have drawn criticism. Debt Justice, a British campaign group, found that four swaps cut national debt by an average of 3%, while ordinary restructurings cut it about seven times more.

A French advocacy group calculated that Belize put $84 million of a $553 million deal toward nature. In Gabon the figure was $67.5 million, with the rest going to repay debt and pay fees.

Then there is Washington. Political risk guarantees from the U.S. government underpinned swaps in Ecuador, Belize, Gabon and El Salvador, and that went away after Donald Trump returned to office.

That leaves private investors to carry more of the load. But getting them to invest means finding conservation projects that can deliver a return, and there aren't enough of those yet. McKinsey cited fragmented data and ecosystem outcomes that are hard to price as two reasons why.

Even if private investment grows, the hardest conservation work may remain beyond its reach. Markets can channel money toward nature where they can extract a return. They are less equipped to pay for protection whose benefits are diffuse, long-term or impossible to monetize.

#5432. This 71-year-old cattleman’s farm brings in $30 million a year. He says the cattle cycle that built it is broken

Cows have roamed Will Harris’s 3,200-acre home farm in southwestern Georgia since 1866, when his great-grandparents got up at dawn six days a week to tend the land. They raised and slaughtered chickens, ducks, hogs, and cows, and would load up the meat in a mule-drawn wagon and drive it up the two-mile dirt road to the town of Bluffton, which had a population of 117 people at the last census, to peddle.

Now Harris, 71, has grown its operations into White Oak Pastures, a 5,700-acre farming ecosystem that he told Fortune is the largest private employer in the county and employs 170 people, almost everyone in Bluffton who isn’t retired or can’t work for other reasons. White Oak’s workforce is larger than the town itself.

“Just about everybody in town that works, works for us,” Harris said.

His business, which raises livestock, processes the meat and sells it directly to consumers, brings in $30 million a year. But Harris says the cycle that built farms like his has broken. Record cattle prices once would have sent ranchers rushing to rebuild their herds. Now the land to do it costs more than cattle can pay for, as investors and developers outbid farmers across rural Georgia. So instead of expanding, he is training new ranchers and is open to a data center coming to his county, because he isn’t sure the old way of building a farm still works.

“I don’t know how this is going to end,” he said.

The U.S. cattle herd is at a 75-year low due to droughts and record-high operating costs, and the price of ground beef, typically the most affordable part of the animal for consumers, hit a record $6.90 per pound earlier this year. Farmland is also harder to buy as farmers are outbid by institutional investors and developers, including the data center companies spreading across rural Georgia. Harris said a data center was approved for construction in his Clay County, but hasn’t started construction.

“If you can get a tremendous amount of money to sell the land, most people sell it. It happens every day, and it’s not just data centers,” Harris said. “The land is moving out of the hands of the farmer or cattle producers into the hands of others.”

White Oak wasn’t always run the way it is now, which is as a regenerative farm, a concept Harris defines as “not breaking the cycles of nature.” When Harris’s father inherited the farm after World War II, he got rid of everything except for cattle and started selling calves to feedlots instead of slaughtering and delivering meat himself, using pesticides and chemical fertilizers to cut costs. Harris went to college and studied animal science, then returned to run the farm similarly for 20 years until 1995.

“I wanted nothing in my pastures except cattle and Tifton 85 Bermuda grass, and if you were not a cow or Tifton 85 Bermuda grass, I would kill you,” he said. “I went to my pastures every single day with the focus of looking for something to kill.”

But then he saw how hard this was on the animals and the land, and changed his approach to reflect “the very old-fashioned way of farming” of his great-grandparents—raising cattle alongside sheep, pigs, goats, and poultry; dropping pesticides; and allowing in more types of grasses.

“It was not easy, but I went from raising cattle very industrially to raising cattle in a very natural manner,” he said. “Now, when I go to the pastures, I’m looking for how to keep everything alive and prospering.”

The shift paid off in the early 2000s, when Harris said “the messaging for grass-fed beef” became more widespread and shoppers started looking for it. That let him put his beef on shelves at Whole Foods and Publix, since the four meatpackers that control 85% of U.S. beef supply had little of it. He said sales grew to about $25 million in 2015, and then the U.S. changed its country-of-origin labeling rules for beef, opening the door for imported beef from places like Australia, Brazil, and Argentina processed or packaged in the U.S. to carry a “Product of USA” label. While Harris kept selling the same volume of beef, his business became unprofitable because he had to cut prices to compete.

“We went from being quite profitable to not being profitable because of that change, and I had a few rough years,” he said.

That changed this year. Since Jan. 1, the USDA has reserved the “Product of USA” label for meat from animals born, raised, slaughtered and processed in the U.S.

The pandemic had already given White Oak a new path. The big meatpackers had to shutter some operations, but also Harris’s daughter came home from college and launched White Oak’s online store with which they could sell directly to customers instead of going through the grocery stores. Harris even opened his first physical store in Atlanta this year, though he has no further plans of expansion.

“We want to do better, not bigger,” he said.

Harris is teaching other farmers to do what he does. He said most industrial farmers can’t easily switch to regenerative methods because they’ve already invested so much into equipment—saying a cotton picker costs about $1.4 million and a grain combine nearly $1 million—and like him, learned how to do it from their predecessors.

“I don’t want to make it sound like I’m doing it right and they’re not and they’re bad people,” he said. “These farmers are doing it the way they learned from their granddad and dad, the way they learned at the land grant university.”

His nonprofit, the Center for Agricultural Resilience, takes six interns per quarter for three months on the farm, and White Oak offers jobs to about half of them. Harris also runs week-long courses on raising cattle and hogs about once a month, drawing 25 to 30 people from across the country and even from England, Spain, Germany, and Mexico.

“They’re frequently young people that are just out of college, or maybe they’ve taken an entry-level job and didn’t like it,” he said. “There are some people who have inherited farms at 30, 40, 50 years of age, and then they come, so it’s all over the board.”

He said counties like his own in Georgia once thrived on farming, but since World War II, companies like Tyson and Cargill took a bigger share of the profits from agriculture, leaving less for those communities. This is why he’s more open to data centers despite having concerns, though he said he’s not part of the opposition because he doesn’t know enough yet.

“These agricultural counties in southwest Georgia are economically impoverished, and we need some other things going on,” he said. “I don’t know if data centers are what we need, but it is some initial relief, and we will see how it goes.”

House of Stake ratified HSP-029 on Nov. 16, and the proposal lowers the maximum annual issuance of NEAR Protocol from 2.5% to 1.6%. On Tuesday, the price of NEAR dipped to $3.12 in the morning and then went back up to $3.26.

HSP-029 was written by Sal Ternullo, CEO of SVRN, and opened for forum discussion on Oct. 7. The vote closed on Nov. 2, and 99.96% of the veNEAR cast was in favor of the proposal; no veNEAR was cast against it. The Security Council's 14-day window to veto the proposal closed on Nov. 16 with no veto, according to House of Stake.

This is the second inflation cut for NEAR in just over a year. In October 2025, the maximum issuance was halved from the original 5% to 2.5%, and in September 2026, the realized issuance stood at 2.45%, according to HSP-029.

At 1.6%, NEAR will have "one of the lowest annual issuance rates among major blockchains," House of Stake said.

According to House of Stake, the reduction will start one quarter after ratification, and validators still have to adopt the protocol upgrade. The issuance cap will reach 1.6% after 24 months.

Ternullo estimated in HSP-029 that NEAR will avoid issuing 11.8 million tokens over two years. At the current price, these tokens would be worth around $38.5 million.

The proposal also calculated that the staking yield of NEAR will go down from around 5.27% to around 3.37% if the staking ratio stays the same. More than half of all NEAR is not staked, according to House of Stake.

#5430. Jeff Bezos has some advice for Nvidia’s board on its CEO search

by Todd Bishop on Nov 17, 2026 at 5:05 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 9:50 am

Jeff Bezos says Nvidia should look inside the company for its next CEO, and he doesn’t give an outsider much chance of success. The Amazon founder, now co-CEO of AI engineering startup Prometheus, made the comments Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event.

“If you don’t bring Jensen back, I would not hire an outsider. Nvidia is too complicated,” Bezos said. Outside CEOs at complex companies, he added, “have a vanishingly small chance of succeeding,” and he would consider hiring one “a last resort.”

Nvidia’s board says it has no plans to bring Huang back. Harvey Jones, the longtime director named the company’s first board chair last week, opened Nvidia’s earnings call Tuesday afternoon by saying the board “does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO.”

Jones said the search will include internal and external candidates, and that the board wants a permanent CEO in place quickly but won’t rush the pick.

Huang, the Nvidia co-founder and CEO for 33 years, had posted a statement on X that morning offering to return. He said he had “made serious mistakes” in his personal life and would cooperate with the board’s independent investigation.

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO,” he wrote.

Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation last Thursday, a day after the New York Times reported that he’d had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reported to him. Days earlier, he admitted to an affair with a woman who U.S. officials believe was recruited by Chinese intelligence, according to the Wall Street Journal.

CFO Colette Kress, who spent 13 years at Microsoft earlier in her career, is interim CEO.

Two major Nvidia investors, Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, asked the board to leave open “the potential return of Jensen Huang.” Analyst Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives wrote in a note Sunday that talk of a Huang comeback is “ridiculous.”

The Amazon precedent (not really): Bezos has been through a founder handoff of his own. He turned over the Amazon CEO job in 2021 to Andy Jassy, a longtime insider who built AWS. When Semafor raised the comparison, Bezos called it a poor one, saying there has never been a more carefully planned transition.

He said he didn’t know enough about what happened in Nvidia’s board meetings to say whether Huang should return. But he called Huang a remarkable founder who deserves “admiration and respect no matter what.”

Huang himself said in a Bloomberg interview recorded Oct. 14 that he hoped his successor was already inside the company.

The Nvidia comments came in a wide-ranging interview. Bezos also said Blue Origin is using Prometheus tools on two projects, called President Trump by far the most communicative of the presidents he has worked with, and said Robert Pattinson was the clear choice to play the next James Bond after screen tests of five finalists.

Business as usual, officially: Nvidia reported third-quarter revenue of $115.8 billion, up 103% from a year earlier, including $107.6 billion from its data center business. On the call, it raised its forecast for next fiscal year’s revenue growth to about 75%, from 70%.

Kress didn’t mention Huang by name on the call. Asked about the leadership transition, she said customers, suppliers and employees remain behind the company, calling it “business as usual.” She ended the call with a short pep talk that finished, “We’ve got this.”

In case the board was wondering about one outsider in particular, Bezos is spoken for. During the Semafor interview, he described running Prometheus as “Nirvana.”

#5429. Jeff Bezos donated $198.9 million in Amazon stock in two days, including shares he’s held since 1994

Jeff Bezos gave away nearly $200 million worth of Amazon stock over two days this month, bringing his disclosed charitable stock donations this year to more than $600 million.

The Amazon founder and executive chair donated 674,088 shares on Nov. 12 and another 97,404 shares the following day, according to a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Nov. 16. Forbes valued the 771,492 shares at $198.9 million based on Amazon’s closing price that day of $257.75.

The Bezos Earth Fund Foundation, which Bezos founded, received the smaller gift, worth about $25 million, and filed a notice of its intent to sell the shares. Bezos acquired those shares on July 5, 1994, the day he incorporated the company that became Amazon and nearly three years before its 1997 IPO.

The gifts come with the Earth Fund’s deadline about four years away. Bezos launched the fund in 2020 with a pledge to give away $10 billion by 2030. As of late September it had granted about $2.4 billion, meaning it would need to average roughly $1.8 billion a year to hit the target, Fortune reported.

The November gifts follow two earlier rounds. Bezos donated more than 1.25 million Amazon shares in May and 415,580 shares in August, worth about $323 million and $107 million, respectively, at the Nov. 16 close.

Altogether, Bezos has donated at least 2.44 million Amazon shares this year, worth approximately $629.1 million at that price.

Day 1 Academies, the nonprofit that runs Bezos Academy, his network of tuition-free preschools, received at least 450,837 of those shares: 220,200 in May and 230,637 in August. Together, the two nonprofits he founded account for about 22.5% of this year’s donated shares. The filings describe the rest as gifts to nonprofits without naming the recipients.

Even after the donations, Bezos directly held more than 878 million shares of Amazon, No. 1 on the 2026 Fortune 500, valued at approximately $226.4 billion as of the Nov. 16 close, per Forbes. This year’s gifts amount to less than 0.3% of that stake.

On Nov. 19, the Earth Fund told Fortune exclusively that it was committing more than $100 million to protect the Amazon rainforest through 15 new grants across South America. Cristián Samper, the fund’s managing director and leader for nature solutions, said it would use grantee reports and independent satellite analysis to track whether forests remain standing and deforestation declines.

Day 1 Academies runs 38 tuition-free, Montessori-inspired preschools in underserved communities across Arizona, Florida, Hawaii, Kentucky, Texas, and Washington. It enrolled 2,456 students for the 2026–27 school year, according to its annual report.

The preschools grew out of the $2 billion philanthropic commitment Bezos announced in 2018 to support early childhood education and families experiencing homelessness.

Through the other arm of that commitment, the Day 1 Families Fund, Bezos funds local organizations that help families move from shelters or the streets into stable housing. In 2025, the fund awarded $102.5 million to 32 groups in 20 states, the District of Columbia, and Guam.

Bezos and his wife, Lauren Sánchez Bezos, had given away an estimated $4.7 billion through the end of 2025, placing them 10th on Forbes’ list of America’s top philanthropists. Forbes put their giving at about $600 million in 2025.

Bezos told CNN in 2022 that he planned to give away most of his fortune during his lifetime. He said “the hard part is figuring out how to do it in a levered way,” drawing a comparison to building Amazon.

“So we’re building the capacity to be able to give away this money,” he said.

His ex-wife, MacKenzie Scott, whose net worth Forbes estimated at $27.1 billion as of Nov. 20, gave away $7.2 billion in 2025 alone. That brought her total since her 2019 divorce from Bezos to $26.4 billion, according to Forbes.

That single year of giving was more than Bezos and Sánchez Bezos have donated over their lifetimes.

Ledger, a crypto wallet firm, said it had experienced a security incident related to Optimizely, a third-party service used on its official website, but reassured its users about the security of their devices and private keys.

Website optimization platform Optimizely said it had discovered and contained a security incident affecting some of its Web Experimentation customers on November 16, 2026. Most of the malicious code has now been removed, with only 1 of the 188 infected snippets found, down from 169.

The main point is that trusted JavaScript is not always trustworthy. A third-party dependency can exploit a website without ever breaking the website's own code or infrastructure.

#5427. Why the Startup Playbook Changes When Your Customer Is a Large Institution

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

In regulated markets like healthcare, a working product isn’t enough — startups must also figure out who pays, how adoption happens, and what to prove before scaling.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Healthcare is the clearest example. A company can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

Venture capital has historically gravitated toward software for good reason. Once a product works, serving additional customers often requires relatively little incremental investment. Companies can test features, respond to feedback, and expand without rebuilding their business at every stage.

Institutional markets operate differently. Sales cycles can stretch for months or years. Products require regulatory approval, third-party validation, security reviews, or integration with existing systems before customers can use them. Even when an organization recognizes a problem, the person experiencing it may not control the purchasing decision.

Founders need to ask different questions — What must we prove before customers will trust this product? Who controls the budget? What existing processes will the product need to fit into? And how long will it realistically take to turn interest into revenue?

Companies selling into institutional markets face two challenges, proving their product works and convincing customers to adopt it. Clearing one doesn’t guarantee success at the other.   Healthcare makes this clear. Consider a diagnostic startup that develops a test, secures FDA clearance, and demonstrates that its technology performs as intended. It has cleared an important regulatory hurdle. But it may still spend months trying to secure a billing code, establish reimbursement, and convince health systems to incorporate it into existing workflows. The technology works, but the business hasn’t figured out how to get paid for it or make it accessible to the people who need it.

As an example, Pear Therapeutics showed how regulatory success can collide with commercial barriers. Its flagship product, reSET, a digital therapeutic for substance use disorder, received a historic FDA De Novo clearance in 2017, supported by published randomized controlled trials demonstrating clinical efficacy. Yet Pear struggled to secure consistent insurance coverage. It spent tens of millions educating commercial health plans and state Medicaid programs and pursuing dedicated coding and payment pathways. Despite FDA authorization, adoption remained slow and sales cycles stalled. Pear filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 2023, and its assets were auctioned off.   This lesson extends to anyone selling into regulated or institutional markets.

Early customer interest is often mistaken for evidence of scalable demand, particularly when a founder pursues a first customer through a pilot. A hospital pilot illustrates the distinction.   A hospital pilot gives a startup a recognizable customer and demonstrates interest in testing its technology. That may look like traction, but it does not ensure a purchase, wider adoption, or recommendations to other health systems.

Founders and hospitals need a shared definition of success. If results take years to evaluate, can the startup sustain itself until then? Revenue potential is often more compelling than cost savings alone. Founders must also confirm whether the pilot is funded and from which budget. Moving from innovation funding to operating funding often requires approval from another team or committee. A pilot may also remain isolated within the system; broader adoption requires integration with hospital workflows and processes—a frequently overlooked hurdle.

Has the founder or company addressed these issues in the pilot? Without clear answers, the pilot risks becoming a costly experiment rather than a path to revenue. End-user acceptance alone does not establish scalable demand, and investors can be misled.

These challenges make the earliest stages of company formation particularly important. Decisions about product development, partnerships, and commercialization can shape a company’s trajectory for years.

At Treehub, we work with founders at this stage, often when the opportunity is promising but the company is still taking shape. We encourage founders to think beyond the technology and understand the environments in which their products will ultimately be used.

That means involving potential customers early, identifying purchasing decision-makers, and understanding barriers to adoption before investing heavily in development. It also means recognizing the value of firsthand industry experience. More than half of the founders in our latest cohort were physicians, bringing direct insight into the problems they aim to solve and the realities of the healthcare system.

AI and new distribution models are also creating opportunities to enter complex markets more efficiently. AI can streamline administrative work and data analysis, while direct-to-consumer platforms and connected devices can help some companies reach customers and validate demand before pursuing traditional institutional channels. These approaches don’t eliminate regulatory requirements, but they can create alternative paths to market.

The traditional startup playbook still has value. Founders should test assumptions early, build efficiently, and listen to customers. But those principles need to be adapted to the markets they’re entering.

Moving quickly without understanding regulatory requirements can create costly setbacks. Securing pilots without a path to paid adoption can produce misleading traction. Building sophisticated technology without knowing who will pay for it can leave founders with a product that works but no sustainable business.

For investors, the lesson is equally important — don’t confuse early validation with commercial viability. Understand what a company needs to prove before it can grow and whether its business model can support that growth.

The most successful founders in complex markets won’t necessarily be the ones who move fastest. They’ll be the ones who understand the obstacles ahead, build around the realities of their customers, and know what needs to be true before scaling makes sense.

For decades, Silicon Valley has followed this startup playbook — move fast, find product-market fit, and scale. For software companies selling directly to consumers or other businesses, that approach works. But when a startup sells into a regulated industry or a large institution, the rules change.

Healthcare is the clearest example. A company can build an impressive product, demonstrate it works, and still struggle to turn it into a viable business. Regulatory requirements, purchasing processes, reimbursement challenges, and workflows can all stand between promising technology and widespread adoption.

The same challenges exist across industries like financial services, education, and government. In these markets, building a product is only one part. Founders must also understand who needs it, pays for it, and what it takes to get an organization to change how it operates.

#5426. ‘You said spicy, right?’ Panel takes on Washington’s economic blind spots — and what needs to change

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:15 pmNovember 18, 2026 at 11:49 am

Washington’s biggest economic threat may be the conviction that it’s already doing everything right.

That was the pointed warning from a Technology Alliance panel Tuesday, where a conversation about talent and economic growth became a challenge to the state’s self-image as an innovation leader.

“You said spicy, right?” Rob Ogburn asked, taking up the invitation to speak bluntly.

“The economy is very strong. The economy is not competitive at all,” said Ogburn, executive director of Business and Community Services at Central Washington University.

While tech giants such as Microsoft and Amazon and sectors including aerospace and biotech are powering today’s economy, that doesn’t mean Washington is positioned to win tomorrow’s investment, develop its workforce or spread opportunity beyond its major employment centers.

Amelia Ransom, former vice president at Smartsheet and past Nordstrom leader, questioned the definition of success, arguing that future growth also depends on investing in people and businesses outside the corporate spotlight.

“Who do we mean when we say winning? Who is it? Who are we talking about, and who are we leaving out?” Ransom said, later adding, “We have to close the daylight between who we say we are and who we actually are.”

The panel was held in downtown Seattle and moderated by Jolenta Coleman-Bush, director of Microsoft Philanthropies. It also included Rachel Smith, president of Washington Roundtable.

Rather than simply calling for more talent and innovation, panelists examined how Washington develops the people already here, whose perspectives inform its decisions and how effectively its institutions and stakeholders work together.

Unification is essential. U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., led the passage of the CHIPS and Science Act in 2022 to bolster semiconductor manufacturing and innovation in AI and energy. But her home state has received just 0.3% of the funding awarded so far, Ogburn said.

He argued that other states and regions were more effective at uniting to make their case for investment, showing their collective resources and the problems they could solve.

“We showed up and said, ‘We’re competing with our neighbor, and we’re better than them.’ No investor is going to look at that and say you’re going to make the best use of my money,” Ogburn said.

Cultivate talent, don’t just recruit it. Ransom compared workforce development to a restaurant, a grocery store and a garden: recruiting ready-made workers, developing the talent already here and growing the long-term pipeline.

“The middle is where we probably need to spend more time, which is at the grocery store, which means you’ve got to learn to cook,” she said. Her point: Invest in Washington’s existing employees, students, and businesses.

Smith wants employers to identify the high-wage, high-skill jobs they need filled so educators and businesses can coordinate strategies to prepare workers for those roles.

Fill essential information gaps. Panelists called for a clearer picture of community skills and barriers to opportunity, more voices to challenge prevailing assumptions, and closer examination of how regulations affect businesses.

“We’ve gotten in this war of the rankings where everybody’s like, “No, we’re the best. No, we’re the worst.” And we we’ve got to stop doing that,” Smith said.

The region needs data-backed insights into the reasons behind the rankings, she said. Smith pointed to the recently formed Economic Development Council and its planned statewide strategy as a step toward a more coordinated approach.

Whether these efforts succeed, Ogburn said, should be judged by the communities themselves.

“And then, if you want to measure success, go back to those communities and ask them if they feel successful,” he said. “Do they have agency and self-determination?”

#5425. Elon Musk’s SpaceX is betting $74 billion on AI data centers. Texas and Arizona want to know who pays for the power

SpaceX wants to build a data center in the Arizona desert that would draw 6,000 megawatts of power at full build-out. That is nearly two-thirds of the all-time peak demand that Arizona Public Service, which serves about 1.5 million homes and businesses, hit across its entire system this summer, according to KJZZ.

The Cochise County campus is the larger half of a plan SpaceX announced on Nov. 12 to spend more than $74 billion on two AI supercomputing sites: roughly $50 billion in southeastern Arizona and more than $24 billion at Starbase, Texas, Reuters reported. The company is pitching both as projects that pay for themselves, with on-site power in Texas, dry cooling in Arizona, and promises of lower bills and taxes for neighbors.

Residents, local officials, and now Arizona’s attorney general want proof first. Who covers the cost of the power plants, water, and grid upgrades behind AI, the company or the people who live next door, is quickly becoming the question that decides whether these campuses get built.

The stakes for SpaceX are large. Its AI segment produced more than half of its third-quarter revenue, ahead of rockets and Starlink, according to Reuters, and Fortune has reported on how renting out computing capacity to Anthropic and Google has become central to the company’s valuation. The political ground is shifting under the industry, too: voters sided against data center development in 37 of 38 local ballot contests with complete counts this month, as Fortune reported after the midterms.

The Texas campus is a gas-fired power plant and “super-compute facility” on 444.45 acres near the Port of Brownsville, The Texas Tribune reported. Brownsville de-annexed the land earlier this year at SpaceX’s request, after the company offered $220 million for city water and wastewater projects. The neighboring city of Starbase, which incorporated around SpaceX’s launch site in 2025, then annexed it.

That sequence leaves the project outside the reach of Brownsville’s 90-day data center moratorium, which took effect in early November. The city says its decision was based on the “information and circumstances presented at the time.”

Because the plant would generate its own electricity, SpaceX says the facility won’t draw from the public grid. It will still burn a lot of gas. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality issued an air permit on Nov. 16 that allows 35 natural gas turbines producing 750 megawatts and up to 248 tons of nitrogen oxides a year, Newsweek reported, citing Politico.

The South Texas Environmental Justice Network has announced a protest, arguing the facilities would pollute the air, use up water, and raise residents’ energy bills. Other residents see opportunity. “There’s a lot of people that need jobs in our community and SpaceX has contributed to those jobs,” Janie Melendez, a Brownsville school teacher who previously served on the Texas Republican Party’s executive committee, told the Tribune.

Melendez has felt SpaceX’s pull in another way. “Since SpaceX moved in, my home has tripled in value,” she said. Rising values are a win for owners, but they tend to lift property tax bills and rents, which can squeeze newer residents and renters.

The tax question is now live. On Nov. 17, Cameron County commissioners voted 3-2 against moving ahead with talks on a 10-year, 100% property tax abatement for the project. Starbase’s own city commission is scheduled to consider a tax abatement on Dec. 9. And in January, SpaceX will face a new governor, Gina Hinojosa, who has vowed to freeze data center approvals until lawmakers pass new protections.

The Arizona campus would sit on 747 acres near the Willcox Playa, about 80 miles east of Tucson, according to the Arizona Daily Star. It would take power from the grid through the Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative and the Arizona Electric Power Cooperative, and SpaceX says the nearby Apache Generating Station, which burns coal and natural gas, would grow from about 1 gigawatt to more than 6 gigawatts. The permit application lists $3.6 billion in planned grid upgrades.

SpaceX’s pitch to the county is aggressive. At a community meeting, Riley Trettle, who heads SpaceX’s energy and supercomputer department, said the project would reduce residents’ electricity bills, lower property taxes by 20%, and create about 1,000 permanent jobs, according to the Star. The application projects a one-time $250 million sales tax benefit for the county and $35 million to $103 million in sales tax revenue, and the company expects about 5,500 construction jobs.

Water is the sharper worry. The campus would be dry-cooled and would not pump groundwater for industrial use, though an existing well could supply up to 10 acre-feet a year for drinking water and maintenance. Residents point to an aquifer already drawn down by large dairy farms, and experts told the Star that the water used to generate the campus’s power could raise annual data center water use by 60% to 90%. The permit doesn’t estimate that figure.

On Nov. 19, Attorney General Kris Mayes asked the Cochise County Planning and Zoning Commission to postpone its Dec. 9 vote until state and federal agencies can review the project. Her letter questions how SpaceX would cover power needs beyond what the regional cooperative can generate, and raises concerns about water, fire safety, traffic, wildlife, and nearby Fort Huachuca. “The people of Cochise County deserve answers before county officials approve a project of this magnitude,” Mayes said in a statement. She plans her own town hall at Cochise Elementary School on Dec. 3.

Arizona’s larger utilities are already wrestling with the same cost split. APS describes its approach as “growth pays for growth”: large customers sign long-term contracts so they, rather than residential and small commercial customers, cover the infrastructure they require, Scripps News reported. Data centers accounted for about 7% of APS’s peak load this year, up from about 5% last year, according to KJZZ.

Regulators draw a finer line. Arizona Corporation Commissioner Kevin Thompson says data centers will pay for any new generation they require, but all customers should share reliability investments that benefit the whole grid. “If it’s for the betterment of the grid as a whole, then that peanut butter should be spread across the bread, right?” he told KJZZ.

Meanwhile, APS is asking the commission to approve a 14% to 16% rate increase for residential customers. In that case, an APS witness, Jamie Moe, acknowledged that residential demand isn’t causing high growth-related costs, KJZZ reported.

SpaceX’s Arizona campus would be served by cooperatives rather than APS, but any rate increase would still need the Corporation Commission’s approval. The Dec. 9 votes in Starbase and Cochise County will be the first public tests of whether SpaceX’s promise that its AI campuses will pay their own way holds up once the bills, and the gigawatts, come due.

#5422. Your Business Is Busy. But Is It Actually Growing? Ask These 4 Questions to Find Out.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

The last quarter of the year is the best time to find out what’s actually earning its keep in your business.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he said, “but you can’t do both at once.”

I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a company.

We tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

I think about Jack’s line a lot this time of year, because the fourth quarter makes business owners a little crazy. The year is almost over, you’ve got revenue goals to hit, budgets to review, and everyone’s already asking about your plans for next year. For a lot of founders, the natural response is to put their heads down and work harder. I’ve done it plenty of times myself, and I’ve learned that a lot of that extra effort goes into motion that never turns into progress.

I’ve spent most of my career working with entrepreneurs building businesses in smaller markets. They know exactly when payroll hits, and they’re building their companies without millions of dollars in outside investment. For them, time is as tight as cash. A business like that can stay incredibly busy for years while nothing really changes.

So before the year wraps up, it’s worth asking a few uncomfortable questions to make sure your time and effort are actually moving you forward.

Revenue is important. I’m certainly not going to argue otherwise. But revenue alone can hide a lot. You can grow sales while your margins shrink. You can bring in new customers who are a nightmare to serve, or hire a bunch of people and add services only to discover you’ve built a more complicated version of the business you already had. I’ve watched founders post record sales and still end the year with less cash and less freedom than they started with.

Before you set another ambitious revenue target, look at what your growth is actually producing. Are you more profitable? Is your team getting stronger? Are your customers happier? Is the business becoming less dependent on you? Those questions will tell you a lot more about whether you’re building something that lasts.

Entrepreneurs are idea people. We love trying new things, whether it’s a new campaign or some shiny piece of software that promises to change everything (cough, cough, AI). I’m guilty of it, too. At some point, though, we have to be honest about the difference between what we enjoy doing and what moves the business forward.

Take marketing. You might spend hours making social media content because you enjoy it, while most of your best customers come from referrals. Or you might be convinced a particular service is your bread and butter, only to find out a less exciting offering is generating most of your profit. The numbers don’t always tell the story we want to hear.

So figure out where your best customers are coming from and what they’re buying. A spreadsheet and an honest hour will get you most of the way there. And if you identify something that’s working, do more of it.

This might be my favorite question, because it’s where founders find the quickest wins.

Every business picks up habits over the years: Meetings that made sense two years ago, reports nobody reads, software nobody logs into, services that stay on the menu because they’ve always been there. Individually, none of these seem like a big deal. Added up, they eat a surprising amount of time and money, and they eat your attention, which might be the most valuable thing a founder has.

Look at what your team spends time on every week and ask a simple question: If we were starting this business today, would we still do it this way? If the answer is no, why are you doing it now?

I love setting goals. I’m a big believer in having a vision and building a plan to get there. I’ve also learned that a new calendar year has never solved an old problem for me. If your sales process is broken in October, a fresh set of goals in January won’t fix it. If you’re spending money on marketing that doesn’t work, a bigger budget just means you’ll waste more of it. And if you’re the bottleneck in every decision, adding more customers is going to make your life harder.

For the first several years of Bolt, I was in every meeting. That made sense when we were scrappy and fighting for every account. As we grew, I started getting in the way of the systems we’d built to run without me. Now the question I ask my team constantly is, “Do I have to be in this meeting?” Usually the answer is no, and the business runs better because of it.

You don’t have to overhaul the whole company all at once. Pick one or two things that would make a real difference, like improving your margins, simplifying an offer, documenting a process or finally handing off something you’ve held onto for too long. Then make those changes now, while you still have some time left in the year.

There’s nothing wrong with pushing hard to finish the year strong. I hope you hit every goal you’ve set. Just don’t get so locked in on a number that you lose sight of what you’re building. Most of us started our businesses to create opportunity and have some control over our time and our future, and a bigger revenue line doesn’t guarantee either one.

Jack was right that you can’t do both at once. So before you lock in next year’s number, ask yourself which season you’re in. If it’s a season to get bigger, run. If it’s a season to get better, give yourself permission to slow down and fix what’s underneath. Either way, choose it on purpose.

A mentor of mine, Jack Nikcevich, told me something years ago that I’ve never forgotten. “You can get bigger, or you can get better,” he said, “but you can’t do both at once.”

I didn’t really understand what he meant until Covid. Work for my marketing agency, Bolt Marketing, slowed overnight, and I was on edge like everyone else. As the dust settled, it became clear that we had enough steady business to keep the lights on, so we made a call. We let go of our most exhausting clients and spent six months working on figuring out who we actually were as a company.

We tightened up our processes and got honest about our positioning — all the stuff we’d been ignoring. We’ve grown every year since, and I can trace almost all of that growth back to this period of intense focus.

#5421. Bezos and Bond: Amazon founder played a big role in casting new 007

Geek Life: Fun stories, memes, humor and other random items at the intersection of tech, science, business and culture.  SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 17, 2026 at 6:36 pmNovember 17, 2026 at 6:36 pm

Jeff Bezos has a space company, a newspaper, an AI startup that’s raised $14.5 billion and, apparently, a seat in the room when Amazon decides who gets a license to kill.

Speaking Tuesday at Semafor’s Silicon Valley & The World event, the Amazon founder said he was “heavily involved” in the casting of Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, a pick Amazon MGM Studios announced Monday.

Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond franchise when it acquired MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, then took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

Bezos said a large initial pool of would-be Bonds was narrowed to five finalists, who then did “real old-fashioned screen tests”: three scenes apiece, in full costume on real sets with other actors.

The other finalists were Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner, according to The New York Times, which reported that the tests took place in London in late October.

Bezos said the decision-makers got together Friday and spent a couple of hours reviewing the screen tests before settling on Pattinson.

“By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing,” Bezos said. “But there was something special about Rob Pattinson and his performances.” He said the group, including director Denis Villeneuve, reached a quick consensus. It was “kind of immediately undebated.”

Bezos admitted that the group was initially “slightly biased” against Pattinson because he’s already so famous.

“We sort of thought, you know, maybe we should have somebody a little more unknown,” he said. “But in the screen tests, it was so obvious he is James Bond.”

#5419. $3 billion Remote CEO told every employee to take a five-hour AI course or miss expectations in their performance review: ‘Get with the times’

With AI coming for jobs, the $3 billion HR platform Remote is forcing its workers to get ahead of it. Employees get five hours of paid company time to take the course. But there’s a catch: skip it and you can forget about a passing performance review.

It’s all part of CEO Job van der Voort’s push to get Remote’s roughly 2,000 employees up to speed on AI.

“AI will run the world so it’s about getting with the times,” van der Voort told Fortune. In his view, employers should get their workers up to scratch—so he launched the free AI crash course, aiforactualwork.com, and made the first course mandatory for his entire workforce.

“It’s very important for companies to take responsibility. They are our people. We hired them. We decided, and then we said to them, ‘the bar now is that you start using AI,’ so yes, we should totally take responsibility for the people that work for us,” he added.

“If you are a company that employs a whole bunch of people, you should take responsibility for the people that work for you. You’re not going to be able to fire all the people that work for you and find new people that are good with this.”

But responsibility goes both ways. Staff who didn’t take him up on the offer would face consequences. “We became really clear. What we said is you have to do it, and if you don’t, you’re not going to get ‘meeting expectations’ in your performance review,” van der Voort said. “So everybody did it.”

Luckily, the threat alone worked, and now everyone in his company is up to speed.

“It just raises the foundational level that we can expect everybody to work at,” he added. “They’re not going to make basic mistakes. When we ask somebody to solve a problem, we don’t have to think to ourselves, oh, but do they know this is super easy with AI?”

Not everyone has a boss who’ll give them hours of paid time to learn AI. But van der Voort says that’s no excuse to avoid learning it.

“If you are an individual and you feel like your employer is not doing this for you, do the course we created because it’s only going to help you—if not with your current job, with a future job.”

He said people have always had to adapt to the latest technology, or get left behind. “People had to learn how to use cell phones. People had to learn how to use computers, right? And this is just another thing.”

And in his eyes, it’s not that hard. “It’s really easy. Just ask the AI, how do I do X, and it will tell you,” he said.

He’s not the only CEO saying you don’t need to be an expert to get started.

Glean CEO Arvind Jain previously told Fortune that “AI is not a difficult thing. You don’t have to sit through 10 hours of a course. Just go into one of these AI tools—whether you want to use Gemini or ChatGPT or whatever—and talk to them like a colleague.”

Orianna Rosa Royle is the Success associate editor at Fortune, overseeing careers, leadership, and company culture coverage. She was previously the senior reporter at Management Today, Britain's longest-running publication for CEOs.
